chapters.title: Chapter 3: Fixed Income and Rates Through the Cycle

lessons.title: Credit Risk in Corporate Bonds: Wider in Contraction, Tighter in Expansion

body.text: A corporate bond's yield isn't just about interest rates. It also charges you for the risk the company might not pay you back, and that extra charge, the credit spread, widens and narrows with the cycle just as predictably as everything else in this course.

children.text: The last two lessons dealt with government bonds, which carry interest rate risk but essentially no default risk. Corporate bonds carry that same interest rate risk, plus a second layer entirely of their own: the risk that the company itself struggles to pay. This lesson is about that second layer, and about how sharply it moves across the business cycle.
Credit Spread: The Second Layer of Bond Risk

markDefs.definition: The extra yield a corporate bond offers over a government bond of the same maturity, compensating investors for default risk and, often, for lower liquidity in the corporate bond.

children.text: is simply a corporate bond's yield minus the government bond yield of the same maturity. A well-rated company might borrow at only a small spread over the government. A weaker one has to pay a much larger spread, or borrow for a shorter tenure, or not be able to borrow from the bond market at all.

children.text: Why Spreads Widen in Contraction and Tighten in Expansion

Recall from Chapter 2 that margins compress in a contraction as operating leverage works against companies. Weaker earnings mean a genuinely higher chance that some borrowers struggle to service their debt, so investors rightly demand more compensation. On top of that, contractions bring a flight to safety: investors who might normally hold lower-rated corporate bonds for the extra yield rush toward government bonds instead, and the market for lower-rated paper can get thin and illiquid fast, widening spreads further, often faster than the actual rise in default risk alone would justify. In an expansion, all of this runs in reverse: earnings improve, defaults become rarer, risk appetite returns, and spreads tighten.
Case Study: IL&FS and the 2018 Credit Freeze

You met IL&FS's September 2018 default in Chapter 1 as a trigger for the pre-Covid slowdown. Look at the same event through the credit-spread lens and it teaches something extra. IL&FS carried a top-tier AAA rating right up until it defaulted, and was downgraded through multiple notches within days as the scale of its debt problems became clear. The shock rippled well beyond IL&FS itself: investors and mutual funds reassessed the entire NBFC and housing finance sector at once, and the spreads demanded on NBFC and HFC bonds broadly, not just IL&FS paper, widened sharply for months afterward. A single issuer's default repriced credit risk for an entire sector.

body.text: This is the key lesson credit spreads teach that pure default statistics don't: spread widening is partly about actual defaults, and partly about investors collectively deciding a whole category of borrower is riskier than they'd assumed, whether or not each individual borrower in that category actually defaults.

children.text: Case Study: Franklin Templeton and the April 2020 Freeze

The clearest lesson in how contraction-driven spread widening can trap retail money came in April 2020. As Covid panic hit markets, the already-thin market for lower-rated corporate bonds froze up almost completely: hardly anyone was willing to buy this paper at any price. Franklin Templeton India held several debt schemes concentrated in exactly this kind of paper, and on 23 April 2020 it abruptly wound up six schemes, trapping roughly ₹25,000 crore of investor money that took a long, court-supervised process to fully return. Crucially, this was not primarily about the underlying companies defaulting, it was a liquidity crisis: spreads had widened so far, so fast, that the funds could not sell holdings to meet redemptions without crystallising huge losses.

children.text: The same story runs the other way once the cycle turns. Through 2021 to 2023, many large Indian corporates used the recovery to pay down debt and strengthen balance sheets, and investor risk appetite for corporate paper returned. Credit spreads across most rating bands compressed steadily from their 2020 peaks, exactly the tightening-in-expansion side of this lesson's title, rewarding investors who had stayed in reasonably rated corporate bonds through the panic rather than exiting into gilts near the bottom.

body.title: A Sector Under Stress
body.scenario: Over the past two quarters, several mid-sized companies in one sector have missed loan repayments, and rating agencies have downgraded a handful of other companies in the same sector, though most have not defaulted.
body.prompt: What would you expect to happen to credit spreads for the whole sector, not just the companies that actually missed payments, and which type of debt fund would feel this the most?
body.modelAnswer: Following the IL&FS pattern, expect credit spreads to widen for the entire sector, not just the handful of companies that actually missed payments or were downgraded, as investors reassess the sector as a category and demand more compensation across the board, and as the market for that sector's bonds gets thinner. A Credit Risk Fund with meaningful exposure to that sector would feel this the most, both through mark-to-market losses on existing holdings as spreads widen, and potentially through liquidity strain if redemption pressure builds at the same time, echoing the Franklin Templeton episode. A Gilt Fund or a Banking & PSU Fund with minimal exposure to that specific sector would be largely unaffected.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: The RBI cuts the repo rate sharply because growth has weakened badly, but at the same time, corporate defaults are rising and credit spreads are widening. What is the most likely net effect on a Credit Risk Fund's NAV?
options: It rises sharply, since falling rates always help all bond funds equally
It is unclear, since falling government yields help, but widening credit spreads on its lower-rated holdings can offset or overwhelm that benefit
It is completely unaffected by either factor
It falls only if the fund holds government bonds
body.explanation: A Credit Risk Fund's holdings carry both interest rate risk and credit risk. A rate cut helps through the interest-rate channel, exactly like a Gilt Fund, but if the same weak-growth environment is also widening credit spreads on its AA-and-below holdings, that can partly or fully cancel out the rate benefit. This is precisely why a sharp contraction is often the worst environment for credit-heavy debt funds, even when rates are falling.

body.text: Duration risk (Lesson 2) and credit risk (this lesson) can pull in different directions at once. In a sharp contraction, the RBI cutting rates is unambiguously good for a Gilt Fund's price, but for a Credit Risk Fund it can be good for the interest-rate component and bad for the credit-spread component at the same time. Never assume a debt fund's behaviour just from what rates are doing, check what it actually holds.

cards.definition: A corporate bond's yield minus the government bond yield of the same maturity, compensating for default and liquidity risk.

The tendency for investors to shift money toward the safest available assets, typically government bonds, during periods of stress, widening credit spreads on riskier bonds in the process.

points: A corporate bond's yield has two layers: interest rate risk, shared with government bonds, and credit risk, compensated for by the credit spread over the equivalent government bond
Credit spreads widen in contraction, as weaker earnings raise real default risk and a flight to safety makes lower-rated bonds harder to sell, and tighten in expansion as both effects reverse
IL&FS's September 2018 default widened spreads across the entire NBFC and HFC sector, not just for IL&FS itself, showing how credit repricing can spread well beyond the actual defaulter
Franklin Templeton's April 2020 wind-up of six debt schemes, trapping roughly ₹25,000 crore, was primarily a liquidity crisis caused by spread widening, not a wave of underlying defaults

Debt fund categories carry very different credit exposure: Gilt Funds carry none, Corporate Bond Funds are limited by a high minimum rating, and Credit Risk Funds deliberately take on meaningful credit risk for extra yield

Duration risk and credit risk can offset or reinforce each other in the same fund; a rate cut helps a fund's interest-rate component but not necessarily its credit-spread component, so check what a debt fund actually holds rather than assuming from its category name or from rates alone
